hints: Focus on how an addition polymer forms, the C=C double bond in the monomer opens up to make single C-C links in the chain.
Split the four carbons in the bracket into two identical pairs, each pair is one C(CH3)(Cl) joined to one C(CH3)(CH3).
Put the double bond back between those two carbons to rebuild the alkene and count its longest four-carbon chain with substituents.
walkthrough:
**Recall how addition polymers work**

Think like a teacher reversing the process. Polymerisation opens a C=C to give -C-C-. To find the monomer, we do the reverse and close a -C-C- back to C=C.

Rule:
$$\text{monomer } C=C \rightarrow \text{polymer } -C-C-$$

**Find the repeating two-carbon unit**

Look at the four carbons in the bracket. Carbons 1 and 3 are identical, each is $C(CH_3)(Cl)$. Carbons 2 and 4 are identical, each is $C(CH_3)(CH_3)$.

So one repeat unit (one monomer) is:
$$-C(CH_3)(Cl)-C(CH_3)(CH_3)-$$

**Rebuild the monomer alkene**

Join those two carbons with a double bond to get the original monomer:
$$(CH_3)C(Cl)=C(CH_3)(CH_3)$$
This is a four-carbon chain with the double bond starting at C2, a chloro group at C2 and a methyl group at C3. That name is 2-chloro-3-methylbut-2-ene.

options.A: Incorrect. 2-chloro-3-methylbutane is an alkane with only single bonds. Addition monomers must be alkenes containing C=C, so a saturated -ane can never be the monomer.
options.B: Correct. Rejoining $C(CH_3)(Cl)$ to $C(CH_3)(CH_3)$ with a double bond gives $CH_3-C(Cl)=C(CH_3)-CH_3$, which is 2-chloro-3-methylbut-2-ene. This polymerises to give exactly the pattern shown.
options.C: Incorrect. 2-chloropent-2-ene is $CH_3-C(Cl)=CH-CH_2-CH_3$. Its polymer would have -CH2- and -CH- groups in the chain, not the fully substituted $C(CH_3)(Cl)$ and $C(CH_3)_2$ carbons seen here. It has the wrong carbon skeleton.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the trap of naming the whole four-carbon bracket section as if it were one saturated molecule. The monomer is only half that length (two carbons) and must contain a double bond.
